text:
Interviewer: Will you begin by telling me your name and your name at the time of the war, where you were born and when you were born?
Interviewee: Okay. My name is Floor Miller now. My maiden was Maush. I was born in Prague.
Interviewer: When?
Interviewee: September 22, 1914.
Interviewer: Tell me a little bit about your family in Prague when you were a girl.
Interviewee: Well, we were just simple people. My father was working and my mother was at home. And we didn't do anything special.
Interviewer: What kind of work did your father do?
Interviewee: He was a company representative, a salesman, in.
Interviewer: Did you have any brothers or sisters?
Interviewee: I had a sister, yes. She was two years younger than I. We didn't do anything special. We just went to school and that was about all.
Interviewer: Was your family religious?
Interviewee: Not really. We went to the temple on high holy days and we belonged to a temple, but we were not religious.
Interviewer: Was your school mixed, or was it a Jewish school?
Interviewee: The first five years I went to a Jewish school. Just for Jewish children. It was a regular school, but just for Jewish children. And then I had to go to the regular school from the sixth grade on.
Interviewer: So your friends were both Jews and Christians?
Interviewee: Yes. But mostly Jews.
Interviewer: In Prague, do you feel like you lived in a Jewish world, or was everybody pretty well mixed?
Interviewee: Pretty well mixed. I went to a Jewish school, but just through the fifth grade. But then it was pretty mixed.
Interviewer: And everyone got along?
Interviewee: More or less, yes. I mean there might have been some single people or so. But pretty much okay.
Interviewer: Do you remember any antisemitism before the war?
Interviewee: Not really. I mean you never trusted everybody, but it wasn't really enticing or anything. Maybe felt it more because he was from a German speaking area.
Interviewer: But it was pretty comfortable?
Interviewee: For me it was pretty comfortable, yes.
Interviewer: Now, as a girl were you involved in any political organizations or Zionist organizations?
Interviewee: Once in a while I went to some Zionist meetings or so, but not really as a rule.
Interviewer: And your family?
Interviewee: Neither.
Interviewer: What were you doing at the time of the beginning of the war?
Interviewee: I had a job with a lawyer who was married to a Jewish woman, so he kept me because he wasn't enticing me and I think he needed me because I knew Czech and German with both shorthand and that was useful.
Interviewer: Prior to the German occupation, did you know much about what was happening in Germany?
Interviewee: Well we heard about it, but we didn't like it so we didn't want to have it too.
Interviewer: Were there refugees coming in to Prague who told you things?
Interviewee: They were, yeah, but not too many that I was in contact with.
Interviewer: So you were working at the time when the Germans came in. Can you tell me what you remember about that day and when was it?
Interviewee: Well we didn't feel comfortable, but since it did not affect me personally, I was pretty indifferent. We didn't like it, but since I could go on working and could stay in my home, we were pretty indifferent: let's put it this way.
Interviewer: Naive?
Interviewee: Maybe naive, yeah. Because, as I say, it was hard to believe so: it was easy enough to believe it.
Interviewer: So when did the Germans come into Prague — what happened?
Interviewee: To me personally, not too much. The only thing, I was working for the lawyer and we had German clients. But they behaved towards me okay. They needed me more or less. I was working for them. I was typing their things because the other girls in the office didn't know how to type German, so I didn't feel too much personally.
Interviewer: Did the clients know that you were Jewish?
Interviewee: Yes, most of them. The ones we were working with did know it and the new ones, when Germans came, we didn't say it. They probably suspected it, but —
Interviewer: Okay. But what I would like to learn more about is — the Germans occupied Prague in March of 1939, right?
Interviewee: Yes.
Interviewer: What happened the day they came in? What did you see? What was going on?
Interviewee: They were marching through the streets. Look today. Let's put it this way, it was simpler.
Interviewer: Was it frightening?
Interviewee: Maybe people were afraid. But I wasn't — personally, I wasn't too much afraid. I know I speak German and what can they do to me. If they need something from me they will come, but I think, what can they do to me? I was naive, but it was easier to think this way.
Interviewer: Were they hurting people? Were they beating people? Were they shooting — anything?
Interviewee: They might have, but I didn't know it and even if there was something going on close, I probably looked away. It was simple.
Interviewer: And your parents too?
Interviewee: My parents too. As long as they let us work.
Interviewer: Now in the beginning did the Germans take any people away or — you know, like they did in some places?
Interviewee: They did, but they did not take away people that I knew or that I knew well.
Interviewer: But you knew they were taking people away?
Interviewee: Yes. We knew it, but what could we do? Not too much. If anything, maybe look away.
Interviewer: Who were they taking away? Was it a particular group of people?
Interviewee: I don't know whether it was a particular group. Someone was in their way or someone wanted his work, or so, they found an excuse to take him away.
Interviewer: So it wasn't rounding up the Intelligencia or something like that?
Interviewee: Not really like this, no. Not in Prague, at least.
Interviewer: So after the Germans came in, did they establish a number of rules for the Jewish people?
Interviewee: They might have, but they didn't touch me too much. So I didn't care too much. No, they're not against me too much. The rules were not applying to me.
Interviewer: Do you remember what some of the rules were?
Interviewee: Not really by now.
Interviewer: Did you have to wear a Jewish star?
Interviewee: Yes. I wore it in the office and when we had no Jewish clients it was covered.
Interviewer: Was your father able to continue his work?
Interviewee: Yes. He was working on — he was a salesman and getting commissions, so it wasn't so terrible.
Interviewer: And your sister?
Interviewee: My sister went to Israel.
